extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers interested in satire, media, and The Babylon Bee
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for producing and assessing satirical news articles (the style exemplified by The Babylon Bee), including aims of satire, target selection, recognizability, platform-moderation risks, and legal/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire's purpose: prompt self-reflection (not just laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The purpose of the site, according to its founder Adam Ford in 2016, was not just to evoke laughter, but to prompt self-reflection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Satire acts like an overhead projector, taking something that people usually ignore and projecting it up on the wall for everyone to see. It forces us to look at things we wouldn't normally look at and makes us ask if we're okay with them." — use satire to surface and critique behaviors, not only to amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting small idiosyncrasies of believers
rubrics_metrics.description: The site 'excels at poking fun at the small idiosyncrasies of believers, especially evangelical Protestants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire can focus on the little habits and cultural quirks of a community; specificity of target can increase comedic payoff and perceived insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lampoon broadly across denominations, politics, and ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Content has 'lampoon[ed] the faithful across denominations, political affiliations, and age groups.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satirical outlet may intentionally cast a wide net in targets (religious denominations, political parties, generational groups) to avoid being seen as only partisan ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial signature: focus on perceived shallowness in evangelical world
rubrics_metrics.description: The site's 'signature hits focus on what the writers see as shallowness in the evangelical world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a recognizable topical focus (e.g., evangelical culture) can create repeatable 'hits' and a distinctive voice for the satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching up / ridiculing cultural power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bee often seeks to 'punch up by "ridiculing every source of authority outside the White House"' and to 'mock people who hold cultural power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire that targets institutions or figures with cultural power is framed as punching up; this is presented as a defensible ethical/comedic stance in many accounts of the site's mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make fun of everybody but avoid hateful content
rubrics_metrics.description: "this comedy makes fun of everybody, but it's a little harder on the left, and when it makes fun of the right it's not hateful."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a norm that satire can be biting without crossing into hate — editorial decisions should aim to mock ideas and power rather than demean groups in hateful ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ironic ambiguity that reinforces readers' biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics say the site is 'adept at writing ironically ambiguous material that lets audiences from different sections of the right reinforce their own beliefs... even if the satire itself should not be considered misinformation, its satire draws on and reinforces actual misinformation and conspiracy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with ambiguity and layered references: overly referential or ambivalent irony can allow audiences to interpret satire as confirming preexisting false beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly signal satire to reduce misinterpretation as factual reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Research and fact-checking incidents show 'people regularly mistook satirical reports from The Babylon Bee... for genuine news' and some stories went viral being taken as real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider contextual cues (headline phrasing, disclaimers, framing) to help readers recognize parody; avoid stripping jokes of context when republished, and be aware that rewording headlines can make satire appear factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptively presenting real-world incidents as factual
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (e.g., the Chick-fil-A Georgia lawmaker story) led fact-checkers to rate pieces 'false' and suggest they were 'deliberately deceptive, rather than genuinely satirical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a satirical piece uses real incidents as a springboard, take care to signal fictionalization clearly so it does not mislead readers about the underlying facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider platform policies and moderation risk when publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bee experienced removals, demonetization, and suspensions (Facebook warnings, Twitter suspension for 'hateful conduct') often tied to platform enforcement decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should account for terms-of-service, hate speech, and misinformation rules on major platforms; expect that edge-case satire may be flagged, demonetized, or removed, and plan appeals/communications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid targeting marginalized groups in ways perceived as misogynistic or transphobic
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and fact-checkers have accused some pieces of being 'ironically' misogynistic or 'frequently antagonistic toward the LGBTQIA+ community.' A tweet about Rachel Levine led to Twitter suspension under 'hateful conduct' policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of how jokes about marginalized identities will be perceived and moderated; editorial review should consider whether satire critiques power/ideas or denigrates vulnerable groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual / referential jokes risk limited accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques note the site's material is often 'riffs on riffs, building referential jokes atop the already referential right-wing commentary about the untrustworthiness of the news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy reliance on audience familiarity with specific media narratives or conspiratorial frames can narrow comedic reach and increase chances of misinterpretation by those outside the reference loop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry labeling and fact-checker standards affect perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checkers created labels (e.g., Snopes' 'labeled satire') to distinguish satire from false claims; the site objected that such labels can imply bad faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that third-party fact-checkers may apply categories that influence distribution and reputation; consider how headline wording and site metadata might affect those assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/constitutional considerations: satire is protected but faces regulatory risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The Babylon Bee has engaged in litigation and amicus briefs defending parody rights and challenging laws (e.g., deepfake/election-speech statutes); courts and legislation can affect satirical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand First Amendment protections in your jurisdiction but also the evolving statutory/regulatory landscape (deepfake, hate-speech, platform-reporting laws) that may constrain distribution or expose creators to legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience orientation and partisan tilt matter for editorial strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The site's tone shifted over time (earlier more critical of Trump; later 'less critical of Trump and more critical of the left'), and editors noted the site is 'a little harder on the left.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial positioning (who you lampoon more often) shapes readership, traffic, and the site's reputation; choose intentional audience/partisan orientation and be prepared for the consequences.
